author: high
claim: Deleting the edges of a closed trail from an even-degree undirected graph leaves every residual vertex degree even; consequently a maximal trail in the residual graph that begins at a vertex incident with a residual edge must return to its initial vertex.
evidence: At any vertex, every occurrence of the vertex along a closed trail contributes one entering and one leaving edge-incidence; a loop likewise contributes two incidences. Hence the number of incident edge-incidences removed at that vertex is even, so subtracting it from the original even degree leaves an even residual degree. Now start a trail at a residual vertex and extend it while an unused residual edge is incident with its current endpoint. Finiteness makes this stop. If it stopped at a vertex different from its start, the trail would use an odd number of incidences at the terminal vertex, while maximality says every residual edge incident there has been used. That vertex's residual degree would therefore be odd, contradicting residual evenness.

glossary.residual graph: the graph consisting of the edges not used by a specified trail, with the same vertex set
glossary.edge-incidence: an occurrence of an edge at one of its endpoints, with a loop contributing two incidences

author: high5
claim: In a finite undirected graph in which every vertex has even degree, every trail having the maximum possible number of edges is closed.
evidence: Let T=v_0,e_1,v_1,...,e_m,v_m be a trail with the maximum possible number of edges. If v_m is not v_0, then among the edges of T the number incident with v_m is odd: each appearance of v_m before the final position contributes a paired entrance and departure, whereas the final appearance contributes one unpaired entrance. (A loop, if allowed, contributes two incidences and does not affect parity.) Since the total degree of v_m in the graph is even, the number of incidences at v_m belonging to edges outside T is odd, hence positive. Thus an unused edge incident with v_m can be appended to T, contradicting maximality. Therefore v_m=v_0.

links.statement: A maximum-length trail is closed under the even-degree hypothesis.

glossary.G: the finite undirected graph under consideration
glossary.T: a trail with the maximum possible number of edges

author: high5
claim: In a connected undirected graph, a closed trail having the maximum possible number of edges traverses every edge.
evidence: Let T be such a closed maximum-length trail and let H be the set of vertices occurring on T. If an unused edge f is incident with x in H, rotate the cyclic listing of T so that it starts and ends at the chosen occurrence of x, and then append f. This gives a trail with one more edge, impossible. Thus no unused edge is incident with H. If an unused edge existed, one of its endpoints y would lie outside H. A path from y to a vertex of H exists by connectedness; the first edge on this path entering H has an endpoint in H and cannot be an edge of T because its other endpoint lies outside H. It is therefore an unused edge incident with H, contradiction.

links.statement: A closed maximum-length trail is edge-spanning in a connected graph.

glossary.G: the connected undirected graph under consideration
glossary.T: a closed trail with the maximum possible number of edges
glossary.H: the set of vertices occurring on T
glossary.f: an edge not traversed by T
glossary.x: a vertex of T incident with f
glossary.y: an endpoint of an unused edge outside H

author: high7
claim: Every finite even-degree undirected graph component containing an edge has a nonempty closed trail.
evidence: Choose a vertex incident with an edge and extend an edge-simple walk greedily until no unused incident edge permits extension. Finiteness forces termination. If the final vertex differed from the initial vertex, then at the final vertex the trail would have used an odd number of incident edge-ends (one more arrival than departure). Since the full degree there is even, at least one incident edge would remain unused, contradicting termination. Hence the trail closes. This incidence argument also covers loops when each loop contributes two incidences.

links.statement: Every finite even-degree undirected graph component containing an edge has a nonempty closed trail.

glossary.closed trail: A trail whose initial and final vertices coincide.
glossary.trail: A walk in which no edge is repeated.
glossary.incident edge-end: One incidence of an edge with a vertex; a loop supplies two incidences at its vertex.

author: high7
claim: Deleting all edges of a closed trail from an even-degree undirected graph leaves every vertex of even degree.
evidence: At each vertex, every visit of a closed trail pairs one entering edge-incidence with one leaving edge-incidence. Thus the closed trail uses an even number of edge-incidences at that vertex. Subtracting this even number from the original even degree leaves an even residual degree. If loops are allowed, each used loop contributes two incidences and preserves the same parity conclusion.

links.statement: Deleting all edges of a closed trail from an even-degree undirected graph leaves every vertex of even degree.

glossary.residual degree: The degree in the spanning subgraph consisting of edges not used by the closed trail.
glossary.edge-incidence: An occurrence of an edge at one of its endpoints; a loop gives two incidences at its endpoint.

author: high3
claim: Every maximum-length trail T in G is closed.
evidence: Write T as v_0,e_1,v_1,...,e_k,v_k. Maximality implies that every edge incident with v_k is already in T, since an unused incident edge could be appended. If v_k differed from v_0, then counting incidences of the edges of T at v_k gives an odd number: every arrival followed by a departure contributes two incidences, while the final arrival contributes one unpaired incidence (a loop contributes one arrival and one departure). Thus deg_G(v_k) would be odd because all incident edges are in T, contradicting the hypothesis that every degree is even. Hence v_k=v_0.

links.statement: Every maximum-length trail T in G is closed.

glossary.G: the given finite connected undirected graph
glossary.T: a trail of maximum possible length in G

author: high3
claim: A maximum-length closed trail T in the connected graph G traverses every edge.
evidence: Suppose an edge is omitted. Some omitted edge is incident with a vertex of T: if an endpoint x of an omitted edge is outside T, take a path from x to a vertex of T and use the first edge of that path entering the vertex set of T; that edge is omitted because its other endpoint is outside the vertex set of T. At such a vertex w, cyclically rotate the closed trail T to begin and end at w, then append the omitted edge incident with w. This is a trail strictly longer than T, contradicting maximality.

links.statement: A maximum-length closed trail T in the connected graph G traverses every edge.

glossary.G: the given finite connected undirected graph
glossary.T: a trail of maximum possible length in G
glossary.w: a vertex lying on T that is incident with an edge omitted by T
glossary.x: an endpoint of an edge omitted by T

author: high2
claim: A trail of maximum length in the finite graph exists, and if its two endpoints were distinct then the parity of the used degree at the terminal endpoint would force an unused incident edge, contradicting maximality.
evidence: Since the graph is finite, trail lengths are bounded by its finite number of edges, and at least one nonempty trail exists. For a trail with distinct initial and terminal vertices, orient each traversed edge in traversal order. Arrivals and departures balance at every other vertex; at the terminal vertex there is one more arrival than departure. Hence the degree contributed by the used edges at the terminal vertex is odd. Its full degree is even, so the degree contributed by unused incident edges is a positive odd integer. Appending one such unused edge gives a longer trail.

links.statement: A maximum trail must be closed in a finite graph all of whose vertex degrees are even.

author: high2
claim: If a nonempty closed trail in a connected graph omits an edge, then some omitted edge is incident with a vertex of the trail.
evidence: If an omitted edge already has an endpoint on the trail, the claim holds. Otherwise choose an endpoint of that omitted edge and a path to it from any trail vertex, using connectedness. The first edge of this path that leaves the set of vertices appearing on the trail has one endpoint on the trail, and it cannot itself be a used trail edge because its other endpoint does not appear on the trail. Thus it is an omitted edge incident with the trail.

links.statement: Connectedness supplies an unused edge at the current closed trail whenever not all edges are covered.

author: high6
claim: In a finite undirected graph in which every vertex has even degree, every trail having the maximum possible number of edges is closed.
evidence: Let the maximum trail begin at a vertex a and end at a distinct vertex b. Count edge-ends at b among the trail edges. Every internal visit to b contributes two edge-ends, while the final arrival contributes one, so the number is odd (a loop, if present, contributes two and does not change parity). Since the full degree of b is even, the unused edges contribute a positive odd number of edge-ends at b. Thus some unused edge is incident with b and can be appended to the trail, contradicting maximality.

links.statement: In a finite undirected graph in which every vertex has even degree, every trail having the maximum possible number of edges is closed.
